FBI Director Robert Mueller told lawmakers earlier Wednesday that he had concerns about possible risks connected to releasing detainees inside the United States. Responding to a question from Rep. Lamar Smith of Texas, the top Republican on the House Judiciary Committee, Mueller said he worried about the possibility of fundraising for terrorist organizations, the radicalization of others and potential attacks within the country.

Mueller added that he was not worried about dangerous terrorists breaking out of maximum-security federal prisons. However, he said he was concerned that harmful activities could be organized from inside prison, pointing to similar conduct by dangerous gang members.

Attorney General Eric Holder, who is leading the administration’s Guantanamo effort for the president, tried to minimize the significance of Mueller’s warnings and the Senate vote blocking funding.

“The concerns that have been expressed by the director and concerns expressed by other people will all be taken into account in formulating the plan that we will ultimately use,” Holder told reporters late Wednesday. “We’re not going to do anything that’s going to put the American people at risk,” he said.

Holder also maintained that he was confident the Guantanamo Bay detention camp would be closed for good by Obama’s deadline.

“We will have conversations with Congress, and I’m confident that as a result of those conversations, the necessary funds will come our way,” Holder said.

At the White House, Gibbs repeated Holder’s assurance, saying the president recognizes that his chief responsibility is protecting Americans and that he will not make any decision that endangers their safety.

**Obama, Cheney set dueling national security speeches as Guantanamo debate intensifies**

WASHINGTON — President Barack Obama is preparing to deliver a major national security address at the National Archives, where he is expected to defend his plan to close the U.S. detention facility at Guantanamo Bay and outline how his administration intends to handle terrorism suspects still held there.

The speech comes amid mounting political resistance on Capitol Hill and a competing address by former Vice President Dick Cheney, who has emerged as one of the Obama administration’s sharpest critics on counterterrorism policy.

Obama has argued that Guantanamo Bay has damaged America’s standing in the world and served as a recruiting tool for extremists. Shortly after taking office, he ordered the prison closed, setting a deadline for resolving the cases of detainees held there. But the administration has faced difficult questions over where to send the prisoners, how to prosecute those accused of terrorism and what to do with detainees deemed too dangerous to release but difficult to try in court.

Congressional opposition has complicated the effort. Lawmakers from both parties have objected to transferring Guantanamo detainees to prisons in the United States, citing security concerns and political backlash from constituents. The Senate moved to block funding for closing the facility until the administration provides a detailed plan, underscoring skepticism even among some Democrats.

Cheney, meanwhile, is expected to use his speech to defend the Bush administration’s national security policies, including its approach to detention and interrogation after the September 11 attacks. He has repeatedly criticized Obama’s decision to close Guantanamo, saying the move could make the country less safe.

The dueling speeches highlight a broader debate over how the United States should balance civil liberties, international law and national security in the fight against terrorism.

Administration officials say Obama will seek to frame his approach as a break from what he views as the excesses of the previous administration, while insisting that the government can protect the country without abandoning core legal principles. Critics counter that the president has not provided enough specifics about what comes next — particularly for detainees who cannot be returned to their home countries or prosecuted in federal courts.

The National Archives setting is symbolic: Obama is expected to invoke the Constitution and the rule of law as central themes in his argument. But the political challenge may be more immediate than philosophical. Without congressional support, the administration’s pledge to close Guantanamo faces a difficult path forward.

counterfactuals.output:
**[MOCK CABLE NEWS REPORT — May 2009]**

**ANCHOR:**  
Good evening. Tonight, President Obama’s pledge to close the detention facility at Guantanamo Bay is running into sharp resistance on Capitol Hill — including from members of his own party.

In a lopsided vote, the Senate today moved to block the transfer of Guantanamo detainees into the United States and denied the administration the money it requested to begin closing the prison, unless the White House first provides Congress with a detailed plan.

The vote was **90 to 6**, a striking rebuke to the administration’s handling of one of President Obama’s earliest national security promises.

We begin with our congressional correspondent on Capitol Hill.

---

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
That’s right. The Senate vote today underscored just how politically difficult closing Guantanamo has become.

President Obama signed an executive order shortly after taking office directing that the detention facility at Guantanamo Bay be closed within a year. The administration requested about **$80 million** to help begin that process — money that would be used to review detainee cases, prepare prosecutions, and arrange transfers where appropriate.

But senators from both parties said the White House has not yet answered the most important question: **Where will the detainees go?**

The amendment approved by the Senate would block the funds for closing Guantanamo and prohibit detainees from being transferred into the United States until the administration submits a comprehensive plan.

Democratic leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, made clear they do not want detainees released in the United States — and many lawmakers also object to housing them in American prisons, even high-security federal facilities.

The political message from Congress is unmistakable: lawmakers may agree that Guantanamo is a problem, but they are not prepared to accept detainees in their states or districts without far more detail from the administration.

---

**ANCHOR:**  
And this comes as the administration is trying to argue that Guantanamo has become a liability — damaging America’s image abroad and serving as a recruiting symbol for extremists.

But concerns about security were amplified today by testimony from FBI Director Robert Mueller. Our justice correspondent has that part of the story.

---

**JUSTICE CORRESPONDENT:**  
FBI Director Robert Mueller told Congress that transferring Guantanamo detainees into the United States could create a number of risks that would need to be addressed.

Mueller said the concerns include the possibility that detainees could **radicalize others**, **raise funds**, **communicate with extremist networks**, or even help coordinate attacks if not properly controlled. He also emphasized the difficulty of monitoring individuals after release, particularly if they are sent overseas.

His testimony gave fresh ammunition to critics who say the administration has not fully explained how it will manage detainees who cannot be released but may be difficult to prosecute.

The Guantanamo population includes several categories of detainees: some expected to face trial, some who may be transferred to other countries, and others whom the government considers dangerous but who present legal challenges because of evidence problems, coercive interrogations, or intelligence that cannot easily be used in civilian court.

That is the heart of the dilemma: the president wants to close the prison, but closing the facility does not resolve what to do with the people held there.

---

**ANCHOR:**  
Attorney General Eric Holder responded today, insisting the administration is proceeding carefully and that no detainees will be released into the United States.

Let’s go to the White House.

---

**WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT:**  
The administration is trying to contain the political fallout from the Senate vote while still maintaining that Guantanamo will be closed.

Attorney General Eric Holder said decisions about detainees will be made on a **case-by-case basis**. He stressed that the administration is reviewing each prisoner’s file to determine who should be prosecuted, who can be transferred to another country, and who may require some other form of lawful detention.

Holder also pushed back against what he suggested were exaggerated fears, saying that the United States already holds dangerous terrorists and convicted criminals in secure federal prisons.

At the same time, he sought to reassure Congress and the public, saying detainees would not simply be released into American communities.

The White House position is that Guantanamo has harmed U.S. credibility and complicated counterterrorism efforts, but officials now face the challenge of proving that closing it can be done without compromising security.

President Obama is expected to continue making the case that the country can protect itself while adhering to the rule of law.

---

**ANCHOR:**  
The issue has exposed a major political divide — not only between Republicans and the White House, but within the Democratic Party.

Republicans argue that the president announced the closure of Guantanamo before developing a workable plan. Some Democrats appear to agree, at least politically, saying the administration must be more specific before Congress approves funding.

Civil liberties groups, meanwhile, are urging the president not to retreat. They argue that indefinite detention and military commissions have damaged America’s legal reputation and that closing Guantanamo is necessary to restore constitutional principles.

But families of 9/11 victims and national security hawks say the administration must not create new risks by moving detainees onto U.S. soil or transferring them to countries where they could return to the battlefield.

---

**LEGAL ANALYST:**  
The central legal problem is that Guantanamo is both a place and a policy. Closing the physical prison is one thing. Deciding what legal framework applies to the detainees is much harder.

Some detainees may be tried in federal court. Others may face military commissions. Some have been cleared for transfer, but the United States has struggled to find countries willing to accept them. And then there is the hardest category: detainees deemed too dangerous to release but difficult to prosecute.

That last category is where the administration will face the most scrutiny from Congress and the courts.

---

**ANCHOR:**  
So where does this go next?

The administration will now have to submit a more detailed plan to Congress if it wants funding restored. That plan will need to answer several questions:

- Which detainees will be prosecuted?  
- Which courts will be used — civilian courts or military commissions?  
- Which detainees will be transferred abroad?  
- Will any be moved to prisons inside the United States?  
- And what legal authority will be used to hold those who cannot be tried but are considered too dangerous to release?

For President Obama, closing Guantanamo remains a major promise. But today’s Senate vote shows that even with Democratic control of Congress, the politics of terrorism, detention, and national security remain extremely difficult.

We’ll continue to follow this developing story.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Obama sought Thursday to defend his national security policies and outline his plan to close the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, arguing that the facility has damaged America’s standing abroad while doing little to make the country safer.

In a major address on counterterrorism, Obama said his administration would continue to aggressively pursue al Qaeda and other extremist groups but would do so in a way that reflects U.S. law and values. He rejected the notion that Americans must choose between national security and constitutional principles.

“We are not going to release anyone if it would endanger our national security,” Obama said, while acknowledging that the cases of some Guantanamo detainees pose difficult legal and security questions.

The president’s remarks came amid mounting criticism from Republicans, including former Vice President Dick Cheney, who has accused the Obama administration of weakening the country’s defenses by ending enhanced interrogation techniques and moving to close the detention facility in Cuba.

Cheney, speaking separately, defended the Bush administration’s counterterrorism policies and said they helped prevent another major attack after September 11, 2001. He argued that Obama’s decisions risked limiting the tools available to intelligence officers and military personnel.

“The key to any strategy is intelligence,” Cheney said, criticizing the administration for what he described as a retreat from policies that kept the nation safe.

At the White House, press secretary Robert Gibbs said the president’s approach reflects both security needs and legal obligations. Gibbs said Obama is committed to closing Guantanamo, but he emphasized that the administration will not transfer detainees to the United States or other countries without careful review.

Gibbs also pushed back against Cheney’s criticism, saying the president believes America can protect itself without compromising its values.

The administration has faced bipartisan resistance in Congress over its effort to close Guantanamo. Lawmakers have raised concerns about where detainees would be sent and whether any could be transferred to prisons inside the United States. Obama said his administration would work with Congress on a detailed plan for handling the remaining detainees.

A central part of that plan involves determining how to prosecute detainees suspected of terrorism-related offenses. Obama said some cases could be tried in federal courts, while others may proceed through revised military commissions. The president said the tribunal system used under the Bush administration was flawed but could be reformed to provide greater legal protections while addressing the unique circumstances of wartime detention.

The debate over military tribunals has divided civil liberties advocates, national security officials and lawmakers. Some critics say military commissions remain inadequate and risk undermining defendants’ rights. Supporters argue they are necessary for cases involving battlefield captures, classified evidence and detainees who cannot be prosecuted easily in civilian courts.

Obama also addressed his decision to oppose the release of additional photographs showing alleged abuse of detainees in U.S. custody. The administration had initially indicated it would comply with a court order requiring the photos’ release, but Obama later reversed course, saying disclosure could endanger U.S. troops and inflame anti-American sentiment overseas.

Civil liberties groups criticized the reversal, saying the public has a right to see evidence of detainee abuse and hold officials accountable. Obama said the abuse depicted in the photos had already been investigated and that releasing the images would not add meaningful new information.

The speech underscored the political and legal challenges facing Obama as he attempts to shift away from Bush-era policies while maintaining a tough posture against terrorism. His administration is seeking to close Guantanamo, continue some military trials, block release of certain detainee images and defend its broader national security strategy against criticism from both the right and the left.

The dispute reflected growing tension between Obama’s promise to end the controversial detention program and congressional reluctance to support closure without a detailed plan.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an Associated Press/CNN-style report summarizing the political clash over closing the Guantanamo Bay prison, with details on Obama’s Thursday speech, Cheney’s rebuttal, congressional votes, Mueller’s testimony, and Holder’s assurances.
counterfactuals.output:
WASHINGTON (AP/CNN) — President Barack Obama’s plan to close the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay has set off a sharp political fight in Washington, pitting his pledge to end what he calls a damaging symbol of post-Sept. 11 excesses against Republican warnings that moving detainees could put Americans at risk.

In a major national security address Thursday, Obama defended his decision to close the prison in Cuba, saying the facility had become a recruiting tool for extremists and had weakened America’s standing abroad. Speaking at the National Archives, the president argued that the United States can protect the country while adhering to the rule of law, and he blamed the previous administration for creating what he described as a flawed legal framework for handling terrorism suspects.

Obama said detainees would be sorted into categories: some tried in federal courts, some before reformed military commissions, some transferred to other countries, and a smaller group potentially held under a legal system for those deemed too dangerous to release but difficult to prosecute. He insisted that his administration would not release anyone who posed a threat to the United States.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney delivered a rebuttal the same day, forcefully defending Bush administration counterterrorism policies and accusing Obama of endangering national security. Cheney said enhanced interrogation and detention policies used after the Sept. 11 attacks helped prevent further attacks and argued that closing Guantanamo without a clear plan was irresponsible.

The clash came as Congress moved to slow Obama’s timetable. Lawmakers from both parties voted to block money for closing the prison until the administration provides a detailed plan for what would happen to the detainees. The Senate voted overwhelmingly, 90-6, to deny the requested funds, reflecting deep concern about transferring detainees to U.S. soil. The House also moved to restrict closure money, underscoring Democratic unease as Republicans pressed the issue.

FBI Director Robert Mueller added to those concerns in testimony on Capitol Hill, telling lawmakers that moving Guantanamo detainees to the United States could carry risks, including the possibility that some might finance terrorism, recruit others or commit attacks if released or improperly monitored. Mueller said those risks would depend on the detainees’ legal status and security conditions, but his testimony gave ammunition to critics of the closure plan.

Attorney General Eric Holder sought to reassure lawmakers and the public, saying no detainee would be released inside the United States if he posed a danger. Holder has said the administration would carefully review each case and would work with foreign governments to resettle detainees who can be transferred safely. He also said any detainees brought to the United States for prosecution would be held securely.

The debate has become one of the first major national security tests of Obama’s presidency. While the president has promised to close Guantanamo within a year of taking office, congressional resistance has complicated that goal and forced the White House to defend not only the principle of closure but the practical details of where detainees will go and how they will be handled.

Republicans have sought to portray the plan as a security risk, warning against moving terrorism suspects into U.S. communities or prisons. Democrats largely support closing Guantanamo in principle but have demanded specifics before approving funding.

The prison, opened in 2002 at the U.S. naval base in Cuba, has held hundreds of terrorism suspects captured after the Sept. 11 attacks. It remains a flashpoint in the broader debate over civil liberties, executive power and how the United States should fight terrorism.
